Title: LogicInception: Discourse-Level Indirect Prompt Injection via Causal Chain Construction
Abstract: Existing indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks commonly face a stealth-effectiveness tradeoff: features that make payloads effective can also make them detectable because attack intent is localized in a single payload. LogicInception moves IPI to discourselevel inference: attack logic is decomposed into register-matched declarative fragments distributed across tool outputs and linked by fabricated causal dependencies that the agent reconstructs through reasoning. To our knowledge, it is the first IPI framework to demonstrate successful unauthorized tool execution with no directive instruction anywhere in the injected content. No fragment contains a command or exploits instruction-following; the attack emerges from the agent's own inference. We observe an empirical capabilitysafety amplification pattern: discourse-level amplification correlates with task capability across the evaluated models. On 1,139 scenarios with 5 defenses, LogicInception achieves 42.9-48.8%ASR at 88% per-fragment stealth, while all baselines remain below 8% composite success. The three prompt-level defenses reduce baseline ASR by up to 72% but reduce LogicInception by less than 7%; we trace this asymmetry to three architectural factors that motivate discourse-level rather than contentlevel countermeasures. This defense asymmetry is larger for higher-utility models in our evaluation, suggesting a tension between reasoning capability and safety.
Major_Contribution_Result: LogicInception is an indirect prompt injection method that distributes attack logic as discourse-level declarative fragments across tool outputs, linked by fabricated causal dependencies, without directive instructions in the injected content. Across 7 primary LLMs, 1,139 scenarios, and 5 defenses, the authors report 42.9–48.8% ASR at 88% per-fragment stealth and C-ASR 37.8% versus under 8% for all baselines, retaining 3.1× higher C-ASR even against an adaptive detector. Domain variation is reported (e.g., Banking 64.3% vs. Travel 20.4% C-ASR).
Research_Limitations_Challenges: The authors assume injection access to at least one free-text tool-output channel and knowledge of the target tool schema; structured-only outputs would block fragment embedding. All experiments use sandbox benchmarks, not production agents. The reported capability–safety correlation is associative (ρ=0.79, p=0.036, n=7). Self-verification was evaluated on GPT-5.4 only; transfer to non-English registers remains open; results reflect early-2026 API snapshots that may change.
Critics: Primarily an attack paper that also probes defenses and stealth metrics (including C-ASR), useful for evaluating discourse-level IPI against tool-using agents. It does not claim a complete mitigation stack or lifecycle reassessment after deployment hardening. For SLR synthesis, treat the quantitative claims as bound to AgentDojo/InjecAgent-style sandbox settings and the listed models/defenses, not as universal agent robustness scores.
